title: The ghost and the curly tail
hookLine: a man gets a ghost who will do any job, but will kill him the moment it runs out of work
carry: seva: serve people as God, and be grateful

lines: A GHOST THAT DOES ANY JOB.
cards: A man wants a ghost to do his bidding. A sage gives him a charm, and the ghost appears: I'll do anything you command. But the moment I have nothing to do, I'll kill you.
The man thinks: perfect. Build me a palace. Done.
Bring me money. Done. Clear this forest.
Done. Every job, finished in minutes. And with rising panic, the man realizes he's running out of jobs.

teach.b: The man runs back to the sage. The sage says: see that dog with the curly tail? Tell the ghost to straighten it.
The ghost pulls the tail straight. Lets go.
It curls right back. Straightens it. Lets go.
Curls. Day after day, until the ghost gives up. Then Vivekananda explains.
The world is like that dog's curly tail. Every generation thinks it will fix things for good, and the tail curls back. So why work to help anyone at all?

teach.h: WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.
teach.b: His surprising answer is the title of that lecture: we help ourselves, not the world. The world doesn't need us to save it. It will go on, with its ups and downs.
But the one who serves is changed by serving. Vivekananda called the world a great moral gymnasium, a place where we build strength by working in it. So he turns charity upside down.
When you help someone, don't feel proud.

teach.h: BE GRATEFUL TO THE ONE YOU HELP.
teach.b: Be grateful, and think of the one you help as God.
That's karma yoga as Hindus live it: seva, service offered as worship.

It's why at many temples the meal served to anyone who comes is prasad, food first offered to God. And it's why a volunteer at a food bank or a temple kitchen isn't failing when the line is just as long next week.
You were never in charge of the tail. You're in charge of the work, and the heart you bring to it. This isn't giving up: his own mission still runs hospitals and schools.

how: The Ramakrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda, runs schools, hospitals and disaster relief as spiritual practice, and its monks and volunteers are taught to see service as a privilege rather than charity.

o: a reward that comes back from helping
action that changes the one who does it
fixing the world once and for all

games.q: the ghost and the tail — tap the pairs.
p: would kill him if it had no work

s: in the story, the ghost finally straightens the tail
it curls back every time, until the ghost gives up.
Vivekananda's lecture is titled 'we help ourselves, not the world'
the fifth lecture in Karma Yoga.
Vivekananda taught that since the world can't be fixed, don't bother serving
he taught serving without needing to win, and founded a mission of service.

games.q: you have a ghost that must always have work, or it will kill you. you've run out of jobs. what does the sage tell you to do?
o: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail.
games.why: it straightens the tail, lets go, and the tail curls back, forever. Vivekananda: the world is like that tail, and our work changes us.

practice: Think of one problem that keeps curling back, a mess that returns, a conflict that won't settle, a cause that never seems to move, and let yourself feel the tiredness of it.
Breathe in and let go of needing it fixed forever; breathe out and hold on to the next small, good action, then quietly thank one person you've helped for the chance, as if thanking God in them.
If you pray, you can offer that thanks.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. In Vivekananda's lecture, good work doesn't straighten the world's tail. It straightens the worker.

orig.note: Sanskrit: action without desire for its fruits; the ideal Vivekananda's Karma Yoga teaches.

carryVoice: Your line: seva: serve people as God, and be grateful. Straightening the tail was never the point. Day three hundred eleven, done.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Karma Yoga (1896), ch. 5, 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World' (the ghost and the dog's curly tail; the moral gymnasium)
